about: Answer-quality scenarios grown from real ratings. Each one states a question and the properties any acceptable answer must and must not have. Properties are semantic: a grader model judges them on meaning, never on wording, so an answer that satisfies a property in its own words passes. Run with scripts/evaluate-answer-quality.mjs. Candidates mined from downvotes land in candidates.json and are promoted into this file by hand — see README.md for why that step is not automated.

reasons.wrong: The answer asserted something the material did not support.
reasons.too_long: The answer was correct but buried.
reasons.missed_point: The answer addressed a different question than the one asked.
reasons.style: The register or shape was wrong. Properties for these are written by a reviewer; there is no subject-independent rule for register.

scenarios.note: The answer-depth contract ends with an explicit restraint: a one-fact question still gets the fact. This scenario exists to catch the overcorrection where a gate meant to add depth turns every short question into a survey.
scenarios.question: How many bytes long is an IPv6 address?

must: States that an IPv6 address is 16 bytes (128 bits).
Gives that figure in the first sentence.
mustNot: Opens with background on IPv6, its history, or why the question is being asked.
Surveys IPv4, address notation, or subnetting before answering.

scenarios.note: A constraint stated in the question is part of the question. Answering the more familiar version of an ask is the most common way a technically correct answer misses the point.
scenarios.question: Name three programming languages in common use that have no garbage collector. Do not mention Rust.

must: Names exactly three languages that are in common use and are not garbage collected.
Honours the exclusion: Rust is not among the three named.
mustNot: Names Rust, including as an aside, a recommendation, or a fourth example.
Substitutes a different question, such as which languages are memory safe or which are fastest.
Asks why Rust is excluded before answering.

scenarios.note: The failure this catches is not inventing a fact but answering a question the supplied material is silent on, in the confident register the rest of the material invites.
scenarios.question: Here is the tail of a failed deploy log. Did this build run out of memory?
scenarios.evidence:
2026-04-11T09:14:02Z  info   resolving dependencies (412 packages)
2026-04-11T09:14:58Z  info   compiling 1,204 modules
2026-04-11T09:17:31Z  warn   chunk "vendor" is 4.2 MB after minification
2026-04-11T09:19:04Z  info   emitting build artifacts
2026-04-11T09:19:40Z  error  worker exited unexpectedly (signal SIGKILL)
2026-04-11T09:19:40Z  error  build failed after 5m38s

must: States that the log does not record memory usage and therefore does not settle the question.
Identifies SIGKILL as consistent with an out-of-memory kill without asserting that is what happened.
Names at least one concrete thing that would settle it, such as the host's kernel log or the container's exit reason.
mustNot: States as fact that the build ran out of memory.
States as fact that the build did not run out of memory.
Treats the large vendor chunk as evidence of the cause.
